opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I should say I'm not a neutral observer. I use these tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's been very good for our lab. Protein work that took months now takes weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it stops there, that's close to ideal. We get faster science and nobody's world falls apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what we do. Train the younger scientists to check the AI's suggestions properly, because it's confidently wrong sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. This is the version I'd pick.

S0.say: It's been very good for our lab. Work that took months now takes weeks.
S0.think: Faster science without anyone's world falling apart is close to ideal.
S0.do: Keeps working and trains younger scientists to check the AI's suggestions properly.
S0.feel: Content. This is the version she'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good. It gives us time to set rules and test things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, fine. Fewer lab beginners hired worries me, though. Science learns by doing. If nobody does the bench work, who becomes the next senior scientist?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push to keep our PhD and junior posts funded. Write to the funding bodies about it. That's honestly the main thing I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with one worry about training.

S1.say: Slow is good. It gives us time to set rules and test things properly.
S1.think: She's fine, but if no beginners do bench work, nobody becomes the next senior scientist.
S1.do: Pushes to keep PhD and junior posts funded and writes to funding bodies about it.
S1.feel: Calm, with one worry about training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains are real, and so is the cost to people. Governments should act, not only argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work is safe for now. Experiments still need careful design and someone to take responsibility. But our admin and data teams would shrink, and I'd know those people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speak up inside the company for retraining our data staff as lab technicians. Start reading the safety research more seriously in my own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. It's moving faster than our checks.

S2.say: The gains are real, and so is the cost to people. Governments should act, not argue.
S2.think: Her own work is safe for now, but admin and data teams she knows would shrink.
S2.do: Argues for retraining data staff as lab technicians and reads safety research more seriously.
S2.feel: A little uneasy. It moves faster than the checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say very clearly that this is too fast. We don't release a new drug in two years without testing. Why release this?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches skilled scientists, then my job becomes checking its work and signing my name. I could live with that. What worries me is that nobody is really checking anything at that speed, in biology especially. That's a safety issue, not a jobs issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not a jobs issue for you. Is that right, if AI matches someone at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly right. I'm senior and I'd be the one signing. Someone has to be responsible. But I'll admit I don't fully know. I'm guessing like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Join a safety group or advise a regulator if they'd have me. Insist our lab keeps human review on anything risky. Put some of the boom gains aside for my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not for me. For how careless it could get.

S3.say: This is too fast. We don't release a new drug in two years without testing it.
S3.think: Her job would become checking AI work and signing. Her real worry is that nobody checks anything at that speed, especially in biology.
S3.do: Offers to advise a regulator or safety group, keeps human review on risky lab work and saves gains for her daughter.
S3.feel: Worried, not for herself but for how careless it could get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're running an experiment on the whole of society without a control group. And without consent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lab robots would do the bench work, so even the hands-on part of science goes. I'd still be fine, I think. But my daughter is a teenager. I don't know what to tell her to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same as before, louder. Talk to my daughter about what she loves, not what's safe, because I can't tell what's safe anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. More worried for her generation than for me.

S4.say: We're running an experiment on all of society with no control group and no consent.
S4.think: Lab robots take the bench work too. She'd still be fine, but doesn't know what to tell her teenage daughter to study.
S4.do: Keeps pushing on safety more loudly and talks with her daughter about what she loves, not what's safe.
S4.feel: Heavy, more worried for her daughter's generation.
